analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal contracts and imposes ten-year debarment on contractors with repeated prevailing-wage violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced beyond a House subcommittee referral, dying without a cosponsor, a hearing, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federal construction projects to pay workers the locally prevailing wage for their trade. This bill would require the Labor Department to cancel the contract of any federal contractor found to have a pattern of violating that law, and to bar the company from winning new federal contracts for ten years, unless the company showed the violations were honest mistakes rather than intentional.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers on federally funded projects, who would get a stronger penalty against employers that repeatedly underpay them.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Labor, upon finding a federal contractor has established a pattern of Davis-Bacon Act violations, to cancel the contract and make the firm ineligible for federal contracts for ten years [S2][S3].
Gives contractors an escape: the penalty does not apply if they show the violations were not intentional but the result of simple and unsystematic error [S2][S3].

Prevailing-wage violations mean workers on federal jobs are not paid the wage the law requires for their trade and locality, so a cancellation-and-debarment penalty creates a direct financial reason for contractors to comply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal construction contractors with repeated wage violations, who would lose their contracts and be barred from federal work for a decade.

drawbacks.text: Critics of the Davis-Bacon Act generally argue that prevailing-wage requirements raise the cost of federal construction to taxpayers; adding contract cancellation and ten-year debarment would stack a heavy penalty on top of that requirement [S2].

A ten-year federal debarment is a severe, effectively business-ending penalty for a mid-size contractor, which could deter firms from bidding on federal work or lead to drawn-out disputes over what counts as a 'pattern' of violations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects a well-defined group—workers on federal construction jobs—by attaching a real consequence to repeatedly underpaying them, while explicitly sparing contractors whose violations were honest, unsystematic errors [S2][S3]. The cost falls on violators and, in the view of Davis-Bacon critics, on taxpayers through higher prevailing wages; the main design risk is that 'pattern of violations' could invite disputes, but the intent exception narrows that. The bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested in committee or on the floor [S5].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews (D-NJ) introduced the bill on May 11, 1998, amending the Davis-Bacon Act so that contractors with a pattern of prevailing-wage violations would lose their federal contract and be barred from federal contracting for ten years [S1][S2][S3].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, and on May 29, 1998 was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; the record shows no further action for the remainder of the 105th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors that repeatedly underpay workers on government jobs faced no new penalty, because the bill never left subcommittee.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill amending the Davis-Bacon Act to add contract cancellation and ten-year debarment for repeat violators.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic sponsor introduced the bill with no cosponsors and no recorded floor or committee votes, so no partisan breakdown exists in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would cancel federal contracts and impose ten-year debarment on firms with a pattern of prevailing-wage violations, hitting hardest at firms whose business model depends on underpaying workers on government jobs [S2][S3]. Workers' gain from enforced wage compliance comes directly out of those firms' payroll savings.

The bill adds a new mandatory penalty channel for the Labor Department and gives contractors a 'simple and unsystematic error' defense, creating both new compliance costs for the industry and a clear boundary for honest mistakes [S2][S3].
